tfn.s: The writer implies that advice to rest more can be unrealistic for some people.
tfn.why: Telling a care worker or single parent to rest "may sound absurd" if they lack control over their schedule.

tfn.s: The writer treats Jebelli's interview as stronger evidence than a scientific study.
tfn.why: The text calls it "an interview, not a study" and presents it as a challenge to a culture, not as proof.

tfn.s: Jebelli became less productive after he changed his attitude to work.
tfn.why: Not stated. The text does not say what happened to his output.

tfn.s: The writer finds the productivity defence of rest convincing to employers but incomplete.
tfn.why: It is "persuasive to an employer, yet it leaves little room for experiences valuable simply because they are pleasurable".

tfn.s: The writer is certain that stepping away from a problem improves creativity.
tfn.why: The text says it "can sometimes support fresh thinking" and warns that broad claims "require caution".

focus.note: Look at what follows each gap: a noun phrase, a full clause or a fragment. Some of these are formal and belong mainly in writing.

speak.title: Role-play: an empty Sunday
speak.setup: Work in pairs. Read your card, then have the conversation. Swap roles and do it again.

a.text: You've got a free Sunday and you hate wasting it. Suggest a busy plan, such as a long run, a museum visit and some study. Explain why you think the day should be useful.

b.role: the friend who wants to rest
b.text: You want to do nothing on Sunday. Say why you need a quiet day and what you'd like to do instead. Try to agree on a plan that works for both of you.

phrases: I don't want to waste the whole day.
Honestly, I just want to switch off.
Why does everything have to be a plan?
Could we do one thing and then relax?
That's fair, let's try it your way.
speak.after: Afterwards, tell the class: what did you agree, and who gave way more?
